messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Certain Songs: Certain songs, Crowding/Overstimulation: Crowded spaces, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Martin Keller is a 56-year-old professional dancer who came to treatment months after a traffic accident in which, by his account, he accidentally caused a serious injury to another driver. He had been driving home after an evening performance, exhausted and distracted, when he misjudged a light and turned into the path of an oncoming car. He remembers the violent angle of impact more than anything else: one car striking another broadside, the crumpling metal, the sudden stillness afterward. He got out and saw the other driver trapped and badly hurt. What has stayed with him is not only the image of the damaged cars but the conviction that in those seconds he did not do enough, quickly enough. Although emergency crews arrived, Martin has become fixed on the idea that he should have prevented the crash altogether and, once it happened, should have somehow protected the other person better.

In the weeks afterward, reminders began to take on a punishing force. If a song came on that had been playing in the theater that night or in the car during his drive home, he felt jerked back into the scene and almost immediately found himself thinking, with familiar harshness, that he had failed in the most important role of his life. Seeing crashed cars on the road or in media coverage had the same effect: the visual impact did not remain just an image but turned quickly into self-accusation, a replay of what he believes he failed to stop. Crowded spaces became especially difficult. In busy theater lobbies and packed rehearsal studios, the sensory overload left him feeling cornered, and from there his mind moved to the same conclusion—that he was the kind of man who had not protected others when it mattered.

Over time, those beliefs began to shape what he did. Martin had come to believe he did not deserve ease or distance from the event, and he also feared that if he allowed himself to stop reviewing it he would be letting himself off the hook. He dwells repeatedly on how he used to be before the accident, comparing that version of himself—a dependable husband, a disciplined performer, someone he thought others could rely on—to the person he now sees as having failed. Yet he also tries hard to push the trauma out of mind, cutting off thoughts when they start and steering conversations away if his wife asks how he is doing. He avoids going near the intersection where the crash occurred, taking longer routes across the city to rehearsals and performances. The avoidance makes sense to him because that location feels like proof of what he did, a place that confirms his belief that he did not do enough.

These efforts have not brought relief. The more Martin suppresses thoughts and organizes his days around avoiding the intersection, the less settled he feels. At night he lies awake, not because he thinks another accident is about to happen in his bedroom, but because he cannot let his guard down; he feels he needs to stay alert, as if vigilance might prevent some further failure. Even in objectively safe situations he cannot relax. During rehearsals he loses focus easily, missing counts or drifting off when choreography is being explained, a change that has embarrassed him in the studio and made him worry about his standing in the company. His wife has noticed that he startles when music starts unexpectedly at home and that he sits tensely through evenings that used to help him unwind.

That constant internal watchfulness also seems to prime the world around him. When he is already keyed up from a sleepless night or from straining to stay composed in rehearsal, a crowded subway platform or a song over the studio speakers hits with greater force. In those moments his attention narrows quickly onto anything that resembles the accident—noise, pressure, impact, the idea of collision—and the trigger lands as if it were happening now. His own state of tension appears to make these reminders easier to detect and harder to shake.

At the same time, the meanings he has attached to the accident seem to widen the field of what can set him off. Because he is certain he failed to protect someone and cannot forgive himself for not doing more, songs, crowds, and images of damaged cars no longer feel like ordinary parts of city life; they have become loaded with accusation. By the time he sought help, he was structuring much of his life around not thinking, not passing that intersection, not being caught off guard in public. What finally brought him in was a rehearsal in which a familiar song came on, his concentration vanished, and he had to step out of a crowded room shaking and ashamed. He told the clinician that he is frightened this is who he is now—a man who failed when it counted and cannot recover—but he is also hoping, cautiously, that he might find some way to live without feeling perpetually on trial.
